title: Sabine and the Sparkly Deception
markdown:
Sabine Leclair was a glassblower, and not merely a competent one. She could make glass spin like a top, hold a rainbow, or sing a tiny sparkly song if you tapped it just so. She was also a grump about anything she could not measure with her ruler or melt in her furnace. Spirits? Fiddlesticks. Her workshop, tucked on a cobbled street that smelled faintly of coal smoke, was a temple of precision. Every tool had its place. Every temperature was recorded. Spirituality, being unmeasurable, was nonsense.

Across town, Madame Orla wore feathers and glitter, and her voice could go whee and boom all at once. She talked to the dearly departed, or at least that is what she told her very eager clients, who paid rather a lot of francs to listen. They adored being elegantly fooled. Her séances were held in a dim parlour where the air hung thick with incense and anticipation.

Sabine’s fancy customers, the ones who bought her most delicate perfume bottles and intricate glass animals, also went to Madame Orla. One day they came with a request. Madame Orla needed spiritual conduits. Things to help the spirits manifest. Something ethereal.

Ethereal meant light, airy, delicate, not of this world. All things Sabine found preposterous. "What in the name of molten silica is an ethereal conduit? Does it have a tensile strength? What is its refractive index? Does it do anything quantifiable?" Her perfectly organized workshop suddenly felt a bit shaky.

Then her furnace, bless its fiery heart, decided to take a holiday. A rather dramatic, smoke-billowing holiday. Sabine needed shiny new bricks, a brand-new extra-powerful bellows, and maybe even a little hat shaped like a flame, just for morale. Shiny new bricks were expensive. Very expensive.

Madame Orla swept into the workshop, trailing lavender and mystery like a flamboyant cape. "Ah, Mademoiselle Leclair. Your glass sings of potential. You make the vessels, and I shall fill them with essence."

"Essence of what?" Sabine’s voice was dry as a cooling rack.

"The Essence of the Beyond, of course." Orla winked, a sparkle that rivaled any of Sabine’s creations. "My clients are dying to be enlightened. The clarity, the way it catches the light. It will be the most exquisite medium for ethereal communication this side of the veil."

The deal was struck. Sabine, queen of precise heat and controlled cooling, found herself crafting shaky glass orbs that were supposed to hum with spiritual energy, twisted rods meant to point to the great beyond, delicate vials filled with shimmering unidentifiable dust. She sighed with every delicate curve. "This orb has the structural integrity of a damp biscuit. If any spirit so much as breathes on it, it will be glass confetti."

Their first big séance. The room was dim, filled with hushed whispers. Madame Orla, draped in midnight velvet, stood by her elaborately carved table. Sabine watched from the shadows, feeling utterly ridiculous. Orla began her incantations, voice rising and falling like a dramatic wave. "And now we shall summon the Great Lumina, he who guides lost souls through the astral planes."

The shaky orb began to wobble. And wobble. The attendees gasped. It teetered, threatening to crash. Sabine’s breath hitched. She wanted to dive forward and catch it, to prevent the ultimate pragmatic failure of the whole charade. Orla grabbed it with a flourish, a theatrical swoosh of velvet, just before it would have made a very un-ethereal splat on the polished floor. The room exhaled. Orla beamed, as if she had personally wrestled Lumina into submission.

Things got wilder. During one particularly fervent séance, Orla was trying to contact some ancient queen who apparently had very specific dietary requirements. Orla’s eyes rolled back. She started a funny little dance. Then she actually looked worried. The spirit seemed to be complaining rather vehemently about the hors d’oeuvres being insipid and lacking artisanal flair. Orla’s usual dramatic pronouncements turned into little squeaks of panic. "Oh, Your Majesty, please do not be cross about the canapés. They were sourced from the finest patisserie." Sabine, peeking from behind a heavy velvet curtain, saw a flicker of something real in Orla’s eyes. Maybe Orla wanted to believe her own act as much as everyone else. A tiny unexpected crack in the shimmering facade.

Then disaster struck with the force of a poorly aimed pie. Monsieur Dubois, a very grumpy very loud critic with a moustache so stiff it could stand on its own, wrote a scathing article. Madame Orla: a charlatan of the highest order. Her glass trinkets mere baubles for the brainless. Orla was a fraud. Sabine’s glasswork was fancy window dressing for a cheap trick. The workshop felt suddenly very cold. Artistic integrity, and livelihood, were balanced like a teetering glass tower.

Sabine could not stand it. Her glass was real. Precise. Beautiful. She locked herself in the workshop, a fortress of scientific certainty, and paced among the glowing furnaces and cooling racks. Then a brilliant idea, as clear and sharp as a perfectly cut facet. She would not make things to trick people into seeing spirits. She would make things to show them the beauty of light. And glass. The inherent magic of physics and optics.

She worked like a whirlwind, fuelled by righteous indignation and copious strong coffee. Prisms that caught every stray sunbeam and spun them into cascading rainbows. Polished spheres that magnified candlelight into glowing orbs. Intricate lattices like delicate spiderwebs spun from pure light that, when hit by a focused beam, cast ephemeral shifting patterns on the walls, spectral dancers or celestial constellations. Not fraud. Stagecraft. Art. Science made beautiful.

The next séance was the grandest yet. The same skeptical clients, the same Monsieur Dubois, who had come no doubt to gloat. Madame Orla, dressed in her finest, took her place, a hint of apprehension beneath her usual flair. Sabine, hidden behind a strategically placed velvet curtain, a small smile playing on her lips, activated her contraptions. Rainbows cascaded across the ceiling. Shimmering shapes danced on the floor like fireflies playing tag. The room filled with a soft ethereal glow, as if the air were made of stardust.

The audience was silent, then they gasped, then they murmured in wonder, faces illuminated by the light. Even Monsieur Dubois’s stiff moustache seemed to droop slightly in awe, his pen forgotten. Madame Orla, sensing the shift, played her part beautifully. She did not claim spirits were talking. She spoke of the energies of the cosmos and the poetry of light, her voice now laced with genuine wonder. Still theatrical, but honest theatre, a celebration of the spectacle Sabine had created.

Sabine watched. She had taken her precise measurable art and added a touch of something else, something that made people gasp not because they were tricked, but because they were shown something truly beautiful. Madame Orla took a genuine bow, bathed in the light Sabine had made, and for the first time Sabine felt a little bit of magic herself. Even a grump who believed only in what she could measure could appreciate a good illusion, especially when it was made of glass. They were a team after all. A wonderfully silly, delightfully deceptive, and surprisingly artistic team.
